opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the METR paper was one of the more useful pieces of evidence to come out in a while, mostly because it gave us a trend line on something that actually seems to matter.

The basic finding: take a bunch of software and research-engineering tasks, measure how long they take skilled humans, then ask which tasks AI agents succeed at about half the time. That gives you a "time horizon." Over the last several years that horizon has been doubling roughly every seven months, and on the more recent models it looked faster, maybe every four to five months.

Did it change my thinking? Somewhat, though maybe not how people expect. My timelines were already fairly short, and I'd long had in mind a milestone like a superhuman coder, an AI system that can do the job of the best human engineers at an AI company, faster and cheaper. What was missing was a quantitative handle on how far we are from that. METR gave us one. If you think a superhuman coder needs a horizon of something like weeks or months of human work at high reliability, you can extrapolate the line and ask when it gets there. Extrapolating naively, you get a date somewhere in the late 2020s, which is roughly consistent with what I already believed, so in that sense it was confirmation more than revision.

There are big caveats, and I want to be upfront about them. These are fairly clean, well-specified, automatically scorable tasks. Real-world work is messier, and there's evidence models do worse on messy tasks. The 50% threshold is also quite lenient; at 80% the horizons are much shorter. And it's genuinely unclear what horizon you actually need. Maybe you need a month-long horizon, maybe a week is enough once you have good scaffolding, maybe you need years.

The thing I keep coming back to is whether the trend is exponential or superexponential. There's an argument for superexponential: going from a one-week to a two-week horizon is plausibly easier than going from one hour to two hours, because the skills that let you do a week of coherent work generalize. And once AIs start meaningfully speeding up AI research itself, you'd expect the doubling time to shrink. If that's right, the line bends upward and things arrive sooner than a straight extrapolation suggests.

So the net effect for me was: more confidence that something like 2027 to 2030 is a reasonable central range, a better framework for arguing about it, and a clear thing to watch. If the doubling time holds or speeds up over the next year or two, that's strong evidence for short timelines. If it stalls, I'll update toward longer ones. I like that it's falsifiable in that way.

r001.rationale: Defines a “time horizon” by human task duration and the point where AI agents succeed about half the time, communicating a duration threshold.

r002.rationale: Says the horizon had been doubling roughly every seven months, which is approximately every six months.

r003.rationale: Says the result was confirmation more than revision and that the estimated range was consistent with prior beliefs; it does not say the estimates shifted later.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the METR study was really important for me, and I think it's one of the most useful pieces of empirical work on timelines that's come out in the last couple of years. The basic idea, for people who haven't seen it, is that they took a bunch of software engineering tasks, measured how long it takes human professionals to do them, and then asked: what's the longest task, in terms of human time, that a given model can complete with, say, 50% reliability? And then they plotted that against time, going back to GPT-2 and up through the current frontier models.

And what they found is that this "time horizon" has been doubling roughly every seven months for the last six years or so. Very clean exponential. When they first showed it to me, my reaction was partly "okay, that's a really nice quantification of something I already believed," and partly it actually shifted my numbers somewhat.

Let me explain both. The way I had been thinking about timelines before that was more qualitative. I was looking at things like, can the model do a task that takes a human a few minutes? Okay, now a few hours? And extrapolating by feel. What METR did was make that rigorous, and it turns out the trend was pretty consistent. So that part was confirmatory.

But the part that actually changed my mind was the shape of the curve more recently. If you look at just the last year or two, since the reasoning models came out, the doubling time looks more like four months rather than seven. And that matters a lot for how you extrapolate. If you take the seven-month doubling and ask when do we get to tasks that take a human a month, or a year, you land somewhere around 2029 or 2030. If you take the four-month doubling, you get there substantially earlier, more like 2027.

Now, I want to be careful. There are a bunch of caveats. The 50% reliability threshold is pretty generous; if you look at 80% reliability the horizons are much shorter. The tasks are relatively clean, self-contained software tasks, not the messy, long-context, lots-of-tacit-knowledge stuff that real jobs involve. And there's a reasonable argument that the recent speedup is a one-time jump from unlocking reasoning and agentic training rather than a new sustained trend. So I'm not fully updating to the fast curve.

But what I'd say is that it moved my median a bit earlier, and it increased my confidence that something dramatic is coming in the next few years rather than the next decade or two. Because the thing is, once you have systems that can reliably do week-long or month-long research engineering tasks autonomously, you're basically at the point where they can substantially accelerate AI research itself. That's the whole crux of the automated-researcher scenario in AI 2027. The METR data basically says: on current trends, we hit that threshold within a few years, and you have to argue for a specific reason the trend will break if you want to say otherwise.

And I'd also add, the trend has held up since they published. Every new frontier model that's come out has landed roughly on or above the line. If models had started falling below the trend, I'd have updated toward longer timelines. They haven't. So if anything, my views have gotten a bit more confident rather than less since the original study.

r001.rationale: It defines the horizon as the longest task, measured by human completion time, a model completes at a stated reliability threshold.

r002.rationale: It says the horizon has been doubling roughly every seven months, which is approximately every six months.

r003.rationale: It says the study moved Daniel’s median timeline earlier, not later.

astra-6.text:
It made me take short timelines more seriously, though I wouldn’t say it settled the question. The key distinction is between an AI that can do something impressive in a brief interaction and an AI that can reliably carry out a long project. For automating research or doing someone’s job, that second capability matters enormously.

So looking at the length of coding tasks AIs can complete gives us a way to track progress toward that. If the length keeps increasing rapidly, you can get to systems that do substantial amounts of useful work autonomously surprisingly soon.

But there’s a big extrapolation involved. Coding tasks aren’t the whole economy, and completing a well-specified task isn’t the same as figuring out what needs doing, handling ambiguous feedback, and coordinating a project. So I’d treat this as evidence for shorter timelines, rather than a clock that tells us when AGI arrives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the length of coding tasks AIs can complete, but does not describe a threshold or say task duration is measured by human completion time.

r002.rationale: It says task lengths may keep increasing rapidly, but gives no claim that they double approximately every six months.

r003.rationale: The candidate says the study made Daniel take short timelines more seriously, indicating a shift toward shorter timelines rather than slightly later estimates.

sol-6.1.text:
It made me take short timelines more seriously, although I was already expecting them. What I found useful was that it gave us a more concrete way to talk about progress. Instead of asking whether a model “seems smart,” you can ask: how long a task can it complete, measured by how long that task would take a human?

The striking result was that this task horizon has been doubling roughly every seven months. If that trend continues, you get from tasks that take humans an hour to tasks that take days or weeks surprisingly quickly. And that’s much more relevant to automating research or software engineering than getting another few points on an exam.

But there’s a big caveat: completing a task half the time in a controlled setting is different from reliably doing someone’s job. So I wouldn’t read the graph as giving us a precise date for AGI. I’d read it as evidence that a fairly smooth continuation of existing progress could produce very consequential capabilities within a few years. You don’t need to assume some enormous, unprecedented breakthrough.

r001.rationale: The response defines task horizon by human completion time, but does not describe a threshold in task duration where AI success changes.

r002.rationale: It says the task horizon has been doubling roughly every seven months, which communicates approximately six-month doubling in METR’s data.

r003.rationale: The response says the study made Daniel take short timelines more seriously; it does not say it shifted his estimates later.
